name: Jaded Media
summary: The website for my own photography and film business. It opens with one line, “Photo and film, let's make art.”, then stays out of the way. Behind the public pages there's an admin area for managing content and video.
highlights: Videos upload straight from the browser to Cloudflare R2 through short-lived signed URLs, so big files never touch the app server.

Security was audited in a dedicated pass: a nonce-based Content Security Policy, HSTS, clickjacking protection, a locked-down Permissions-Policy, link-scheme checks on rendered markdown, and an hourly cap on admin email sending.
Legal, privacy, cookie-consent and accessibility work got its own phase, and it's documented.
Runs on a custom domain, and every branch gets a preview deployment before anything reaches production.

name: Edgeline Exports
summary: Site for an online-only dealership that buys, sells and sources performance and luxury cars across Canada and the US. You can browse inventory, ask for a specific car to be found, or offer yours for sale.
highlights: Three customer paths, each with its own page and form: buy from inventory, have a car sourced, or sell to the dealership.
The whole site switches between English and French and between light and dark themes.
Search and sharing are covered: structured data for the business, a generated share image, a sitemap, and a robots file that keeps the admin and API routes out of search.
A separate admin login for the owner, loading states, and a friendly 404 for sold or missing listings.

name: NitroDrp
kind: Private file transfer app on AWS
summary: I got tired of paying for WeTransfer, so I built a prettier one. You upload big files, get an unguessable link, and pick an expiry, an optional password and a download limit. It runs on AWS from end to end: a Lightsail server for the app, S3 for the files, DynamoDB for the links and SES for emailing them. The live demo runs entirely in your browser, so nothing is actually uploaded.
highlights: File bytes never touch my server. The API only signs URLs, and the browser sends 16 MiB parts straight to S3, so multi-GB files work. Each part retries and the upload resumes after a reload.
Links expire on their own. The API refuses expired links, DynamoDB TTL deletes the metadata and S3 lifecycle rules delete the files, so there's no cleanup job.
Download limits can't be beaten by racing. The count is one conditional database write, and a concurrency test backs it up.
It runs on a small always-on Lightsail server behind Caddy with automatic HTTPS. Terraform builds the AWS side, with its state in its own versioned S3 bucket.
Links can be emailed through Amazon SES. The sender gets the replies, the password is never in the email, and each link has a cap on how many it can send.
Sign in with Face ID or a fingerprint (passkeys) and see the same links on your phone and laptop. It also installs on a phone as a home-screen app.
“Download all” streams a .zip on the fly in flat memory, checked with a 4.8 GB archive.

name: Opus
kind: Personal assistant for my inbox and subscriptions
summary: Opus is a personal assistant I built for my own email and subscriptions. It sorts my inbox, flags what needs a reply, drafts the replies, keeps an eye on what I'm paying for and puts anything with consequences in an approval queue. It never sends, deletes or cancels anything by itself. The demo here is a separate public build with made-up sample data and no server behind it. The real assistant is private and runs behind Tailscale.
highlights: It can't send, delete, trash, label or cancel anything. The model only gets the tools in one file, none of them do those things, and a check script (npm run safety) fails if that changes.
Anything with consequences waits in an approval queue. Approving only makes Opus write out the steps for me. It still never cancels or sends for me.
It drafts replies into Gmail Drafts and flags what needs an answer, so I read and send them myself.
It watches its own cost. Cheap triage runs on Haiku, drafts run on Sonnet, bulk senders are sorted by plain rules for free, and there's a per-run cap and a spending alert.
The real one runs behind Tailscale with no port open to the internet, and the dashboard installs on an iPhone as a web app.
The demo on this site is a static build with sample data. It makes no network calls, so nothing in it is my real email or money.

name: This portfolio
kind: Personal portfolio with an admin backend
summary: The site you're on. It shows my other work in live previews, lists my certifications with links to the official records, and has a private admin page so I can add things without touching code.
highlights: The previews are the real sites loaded in scaled frames, with a desktop and mobile toggle, so a visitor sees the actual work instead of screenshots.
Certifications are managed from a password-protected admin page that supports file upload, editing and deletion, and every entry links to the issuer's official record or the uploaded certificate.
The backend checks everything it receives: uploads are identified by their contents, links must be https, and admin actions need a signed session cookie plus a request header.
More than twenty automated tests and an end-to-end browser run cover login, uploads, validation, public pages and the security checks.
